claim: Clec11a was significantly more highly expressed by Scf-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts as compared to VE-cadherin+ endothelial cells and unfractionated cells.
source: Reanalysis of our published microarray data (Ding et al., 2012) revealed that among enzymatically dissociated bone marrow cells, Clec11a was significantly more highly expressed by Scf-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells (more than 90% of which are also LepR+ [Zhou et al., 2014a]) and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts as compared to VE-cadherin+ endothelial cells and unfractionated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 1A and referenced to published data (Ding et al., 2012).

claim: More than 90% of Scf-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells are also LepR+.
source: Clec11a was significantly more highly expressed by Scf-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells (more than 90% of which are also LepR+ [Zhou et al., 2014a])
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2014a.

claim: Clec11a transcripts were at least 100-fold more abundant in PDGFRα+CD45-Ter119-CD31- bone marrow stromal cells as compared to unfractionated bone marrow cells.
source: By RNA sequencing, Clec11a transcripts were at least 100-fold more abundant in PDGFRα+CD45-Ter119-CD31- bone marrow stromal cells (more than 90% of which are LepR+ [Zhou et al., 2014a]) as compared to unfractionated bone marrow cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: More than 90% of PDGFRα+CD45-Ter119-CD31- bone marrow stromal cells are LepR+.
source: By RNA sequencing, Clec11a transcripts were at least 100-fold more abundant in PDGFRα+CD45-Ter119-CD31- bone marrow stromal cells (more than 90% of which are LepR+ [Zhou et al., 2014a]) as compared to unfractionated bone marrow cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2014a.

claim: Clec11a was highly expressed by LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts but not by hematopoietic cells.
source: A systematic analysis of Clec11a expression in bone marrow cells by quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) showed that Clec11a was highly expressed by LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts but not by hematopoietic cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Clec11a was expressed at a very low level by B cell progenitors in the bone marrow and T cells in the spleen.
source: Clec11a was also expressed at a very low level by B cell progenitors in the bone marrow and T cells in the spleen (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RNA-seq analysis showed 80-fold higher levels of Clec11a in bone fragments that contain osteoblasts and osteocytes as compared to whole bone marrow or skeletal muscle cells.
source: Published gene expression profile data were consistent with our results. RNA-seq analysis showed 80-fold higher levels of Clec11a in bone fragments that contain osteoblasts and osteocytes as compared to whole bone marrow or skeletal muscle cells (Ayturk et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published RNA-seq data (Ayturk et al., 2013).

claim: Clec11a expression is 9-fold higher in Grem1+ SSCs as compared to Grem1- stromal cells.
source: Clec11a expression is 9-fold higher in Grem1+ SSCs as compared to Grem1- stromal cells (see GSE57729 from [Worthley et al., 2015]).
evidence: Supported by citation to published gene expression data (Worthley et al., 2015).

claim: LepR+ stromal cells are enriched for Grem1 expression.
source: LepR+ stromal cells are enriched for Grem1 expression (see GSE33158 from [Ding et al., 2012]).
evidence: Supported by citation to published gene expression data (Ding et al., 2012).

claim: Most of the Clec11a staining was observed in and around the trabecular bone in the femur metaphysis in two month-old mice.
source: In two month-old mice, most of the Clec11a staining was observed in and around the trabecular bone in the femur metaphysis (Figure 1F) as well as in cortical bone of the proximal femur (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1F and 1H.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed in cortical bone of the proximal femur in two month-old mice.
source: In two month-old mice, most of the Clec11a staining was observed in and around the trabecular bone in the femur metaphysis (Figure 1F) as well as in cortical bone of the proximal femur (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1H.

claim: No Clec11a staining was observed in bone marrow sections from Clec11a deficient mice.
source: This staining pattern was specific for Clec11a as we did not observe any staining in bone marrow sections from Clec11a deficient mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; see below) or in sections stained with an isotype control in place of the anti-Clec11a antibody (Figure 1E,G, and I).
evidence: Supported by negative control staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed adjacent to Tomato+ stromal cells in the bone marrow near trabecular bone in the distal femur metaphysis of Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice.
source: Within the distal femur metaphysis of Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice we observed Clec11a staining adjacent to Tomato+ stromal cells in the bone marrow near trabecular bone (Figure 1Fi)
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1Fi.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed in Tomato+ osteoblasts lining trabecular bone surfaces in Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice.
source: Within the distal femur metaphysis of Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice we observed Clec11a staining adjacent to Tomato+ stromal cells in the bone marrow near trabecular bone (Figure 1Fi), Tomato+ osteoblasts lining trabecular bone surfaces (Figure 1Fii)
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1Fii.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed in Aggrecan+ hypertrophic chondrocytes in Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice.
source: Within the distal femur metaphysis of Prrx1-Cre; tdTomato mice we observed Clec11a staining adjacent to Tomato+ stromal cells in the bone marrow near trabecular bone (Figure 1Fi), Tomato+ osteoblasts lining trabecular bone surfaces (Figure 1Fii), and Aggrecan+ hypertrophic chondrocytes (Figure 1Fiii; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1Fiii and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed amongst osteocytes in the cortical bone matrix.
source: In the cortical bone matrix, we also observed Clec11a staining amongst osteocytes (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Clec11a expression was not detected by bone marrow stromal cells, osteoblasts, or osteocytes in much of the diaphysis.
source: We did not detect Clec11a expression by bone marrow stromal cells, osteoblasts, or osteocytes in much of the diaphysis.
evidence: Based on absence of antibody staining in diaphysis regions.

claim: Clec11a staining was observed adjacent to a subset of Tomato+ stromal cells near trabecular bone in the metaphysis of Lepr-Cre; tdTomato mice.
source: To test this, we stained femur sections from eight week-old Lepr-Cre; tdTomato mice with anti-Clec11a antibody. We observed Clec11a staining adjacent to a subset of Tomato+ stromal cells near trabecular bone in the metaphysis (Figure 1J) but not by Tomato+ stromal cells throughout most of the diaphysis.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Clec11a staining was not observed by Tomato+ stromal cells throughout most of the diaphysis in Lepr-Cre; tdTomato mice.
source: We observed Clec11a staining adjacent to a subset of Tomato+ stromal cells near trabecular bone in the metaphysis (Figure 1J) but not by Tomato+ stromal cells throughout most of the diaphysis.
evidence: Based on absence of staining in diaphysis regions.

claim: Clec11a staining in LepR+ cells in the metaphysis was clearly above background.
source: The Clec11a staining in LepR+ cells in the metaphysis (Figure 1J) was clearly above background (Figure 1I) but was dimmer than observed in and around bone matrix (Figure 1F and H).
evidence: Supported by comparison of staining intensity in Figure 1J versus Figure 1I (isotype control).

claim: Clec11a staining in LepR+ cells in the metaphysis was dimmer than observed in and around bone matrix.
source: The Clec11a staining in LepR+ cells in the metaphysis (Figure 1J) was clearly above background (Figure 1I) but was dimmer than observed in and around bone matrix (Figure 1F and H).
evidence: Supported by comparison of staining intensity in Figure 1J versus Figure 1F and H.

claim: A similar Clec11a expression pattern was observed in vertebrae, with anti-Clec11a antibody staining in and around the vertebral trabecular bone near the growth plate as well as in cortical bone.
source: We observed a similar Clec11a expression pattern in vertebrae, with anti-Clec11a antibody staining in and around the vertebral trabecular bone near the growth plate as well as in cortical bone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Clec11a is expressed by subsets of LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells, osteoblasts, and hypertrophic chondrocytes in the metaphysis as well as by osteocytes in certain regions of cortical bone.
source: Our data thus indicate that Clec11a is expressed by subsets of LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells, osteoblasts, and hypertrophic chondrocytes in the metaphysis as well as by osteocytes in certain regions of cortical bone.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple immunofluorescence staining experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of exon 2 in Clec11a introduced a frame shift that created a premature stop codon in exon 3.
source: This was predicted to be a strong loss of function as exon 2 deletion introduced a frame shift that created a premature stop codon in exon 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The predicted mutant Clec11a protein did not contain any of the domains that are thought to be functionally important in Clec11a, including the polyglutamic acid sequence, the alpha-helical leucine zipper, or the C-type lectin domain.
source: The predicted mutant protein did not contain any of the domains that are thought to be functionally important in Clec11a, including the polyglutamic acid sequence, the alpha-helical leucine zipper, or the C-type lectin domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by protein structure analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Germline transmission of the mutant Clec11a allele was confirmed by PCR and sequencing of genomic DNA.
source: Germline transmission of the mutant allele was confirmed by PCR and sequencing of genomic DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Clec11a deficiency was confirmed by qPCR analysis of bone marrow LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- cells from Clec11a-/- mice.
source: Clec11a deficiency was also confirmed by qPCR analysis of bone marrow LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- cells from Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Clec11a deficiency was confirmed by Clec11a cDNA sequencing to confirm exon two deletion.
source: Clec11a deficiency was also confirmed by qPCR analysis of bone marrow LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- cells from Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and by Clec11a cDNA sequencing to confirm exon two deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: Supported by cDNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Clec11a was lost from the plasma of Clec11a-/- mice.
source: Clec11a deficiency was also confirmed by qPCR analysis of bone marrow LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- cells from Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and by Clec11a cDNA sequencing to confirm exon two deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and by the loss of Clec11a from the plasma Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of femur sections with an anti-Clec11a polyclonal antibody suggested a complete loss of Clec11a protein from Clec11a-/- mice.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of femur sections with an anti-Clec11a polyclonal antibody suggested a complete loss of Clec11a protein from Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice were born with Mendelian frequency.
source: Clec11a-/- mice were born with Mendelian frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K)
evidence: Supported by genotype frequency data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice appeared grossly normal.
source: Clec11a-/- mice were born with Mendelian frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K) and appeared grossly normal (Figure 1K)
evidence: Supported by visual observation shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice had normal body mass at 2 and 10 months of age.
source: Clec11a-/- mice were born with Mendelian frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K) and appeared grossly normal (Figure 1K), with normal body mass at 2 and 10 months of age (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by body mass measurements shown in Figure 1L.

claim: White blood cell, red blood cell, and platelet counts were normal in 2, 10, and 16 month-old Clec11a-/- mice.
source: White blood cell, red blood cell, and platelet counts were normal in 2, 10, and 16 month-old Clec11a-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–N).
evidence: Supported by blood count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–N.

claim: Two and 10-month old Clec11a-/- mice had normal bone marrow and spleen cellularity.
source: Two and 10-month old Clec11a-/- mice also had normal bone marrow and spleen cellularity (Figure 1M)
evidence: Supported by cellularity measurements shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice had normal frequencies of Mac1+Gr1+ myeloid cells, Ter119+CD71+ erythroid progenitors, CD3+ T cells, and B220+ B cells in the bone marrow and spleen.
source: Two and 10-month old Clec11a-/- mice also had normal bone marrow and spleen cellularity (Figure 1M), as well as normal frequencies of Mac1+Gr1+ myeloid cells, Ter119+CD71+ erythroid progenitors, CD3+ T cells, and B220+ B cells in the bone marrow and spleen (Figure 1N–Q).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1N–Q.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice had normal frequencies of CD150+CD48-Lineage-Sca-1+c-kit+ HSCs and CD150-CD48-Lin-Sca-1+c-kit+multipotent progenitors (MPPs) in the bone marrow and spleen.
source: Clec11a-/- mice had normal frequencies of CD150+CD48-Lineage-Sca-1+c-kit+ HSCs (Kiel et al., 2005) and CD150-CD48-Lin-Sca-1+c-kit+multipotent progenitors (MPPs) (Kiel et al., 2008; Oguro et al., 2013) in the bone marrow and spleen (Figure 1R and S)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1R and S, with cell population definitions from cited references.

claim: Bone marrow from two month-old Clec11a-/- mice gave long-term multilineage reconstitution upon transplantation into irradiated mice with normal levels of donor cell reconstitution.
source: Bone marrow from two month-old Clec11a-/- mice gave long-term multilineage reconstitution upon transplantation into irradiated mice with normal levels of donor cell reconstitution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O–R).
evidence: Supported by competitive reconstitution assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O–R.

claim: Clec11a is not required for normal hematopoiesis in adult mice.
source: Clec11a is therefore not required for normal hematopoiesis in adult mice.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple hematopoietic analyses showing no defects in Clec11a-/- mice.

claim: Human recombinant Clec11a increases erythroid (BFU-E) and myeloid (CFU-G/M/GM) colony formation by human bone marrow cells when added to culture along with EPO or GM-CSF, respectively.
source: Human recombinant Clec11a increases erythroid (BFU-E) and myeloid (CFU-G/M/GM) colony formation by human bone marrow cells when added to culture along with EPO or GM-CSF, respectively (Hiraoka et al., 1997, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Hiraoka et al., 1997, 2001).

claim: Recombinant mouse Clec11a did not significantly increase BFU-E colony formation when added along with EPO in cultures of mouse bone marrow cells.
source: In cultures of mouse bone marrow cells, recombinant mouse Clec11a did not significantly increase BFU-E colony formation when added along with EPO and only slightly increased CFU-G/M/GM colony formation when added along with GM-CSF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S and T).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S and T.

claim: Recombinant mouse Clec11a only slightly increased CFU-G/M/GM colony formation when added along with GM-CSF in cultures of mouse bone marrow cells.
source: In cultures of mouse bone marrow cells, recombinant mouse Clec11a did not significantly increase BFU-E colony formation when added along with EPO and only slightly increased CFU-G/M/GM colony formation when added along with GM-CSF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S and T).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S and T.

claim: Trabecular bone volume was significantly reduced (by 24 ± 18%) in two month-old Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls.
source: Trabecular bone volume was significantly reduced (by 24 ± 18%) in two month-old Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 2A and D.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice had significantly reduced trabecular bone thickness, increased trabecular spacing, and decreased connectively density and bone mineral density.
source: The Clec11a-/- mice had significantly reduced trabecular bone thickness, increased trabecular spacing, and decreased connectively density and bone mineral density (Figure 2D–I).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 2D–I.

claim: The bone defects in Clec11a-/- mice seemed to worsen with age as 10 and 16 month-old Clec11a-/- mice exhibited more profound reductions in trabecular bone volume (62 ± 27% and 64 ± 11%, respectively), trabecular number, trabecular thickness and connectivity density, as well as increased trabecular spacing.
source: With the exception of the reduction in bone mineral density, these defects seemed to worsen with age as 10 and 16 month-old Clec11a-/- mice exhibited more profound reductions in trabecular bone volume (62 ± 27% and 64 ± 11%, respectively), trabecular number, trabecular thickness and connectivity density, as well as increased trabecular spacing (Figure 2B–H).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 2B–H comparing different age groups.

claim: Alizarin red/alcian blue double staining at postnatal day 3 did not reveal any significant differences between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice.
source: Alizarin red/alcian blue double staining at postnatal day 3 did not reveal any significant differences between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1S).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1S.

claim: Clec11a is not required for fetal skeletal development.
source: This suggests that Clec11a is not required for fetal skeletal development.
evidence: Inference based on normal skeletal staining at postnatal day 3.

claim: The trabecular bone mineral apposition and trabecular bone formation rates were both significantly decreased in the femur metaphysis of 2 and 10 month-old Clec11a-/- as compared to sex-matched littermate control mice.
source: The trabecular bone mineral apposition and trabecular bone formation rates were both significantly decreased in the femur metaphysis of 2 and 10 month-old Clec11a-/- as compared to sex-matched littermate control mice (Figure 2T and U; 16 month-old mice were not assessed in these experiments).
evidence: Supported by calcein double labeling data shown in Figure 2T and U.

claim: The urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and littermate controls.
source: In contrast, the urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and littermate controls (Figure 2V).
evidence: Supported by bone resorption analysis shown in Figure 2V.

claim: The difference in trabecular bone volume between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice reflected reduced bone formation, not a change in bone resorption.
source: This suggests that the difference in trabecular bone volume between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice reflected reduced bone formation, not a change in bone resorption.
evidence: Inference based on reduced bone formation rate but unchanged bone resorption marker.

claim: The frequency of LepR+CD45-Ter119-Tie2- stromal cells did not significantly differ between the bone marrow of Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice.
source: The frequency of LepR+CD45-Ter119-Tie2- stromal cells did not significantly differ between the bone marrow of Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no difference in the rate of BrdU incorporation by LepR+CD45-Ter119-Tie2- stromal cells in vivo between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice.
source: We also did not detect any difference in the rate of BrdU incorporation by these cells in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) or the percentage of these cells that stained positively for activated caspase 3/7 (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There was no difference in the percentage of LepR+CD45-Ter119-Tie2- stromal cells that stained positively for activated caspase 3/7 between Clec11a-/- and littermate control mice.
source: We also did not detect any difference in the rate of BrdU incorporation by these cells in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) or the percentage of these cells that stained positively for activated caspase 3/7 (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as data not shown.

claim: Nearly all CD51+ bone marrow stromal cells were LepR+ and vice versa in 10 month-old bone marrow.
source: All of these cell populations were uniformly or nearly uniformly positive for LeprR expression as nearly all CD51+ bone marrow stromal cells were LepR+ and vice versa (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Clec11a deficiency did not affect the frequency of mesenchymal stem and progenitor cell populations identified based on CD51 and other markers.
source: Consistent with the data on LepR+ cells above, we did not detect any effect of Clec11a deficiency on the frequency of these cell populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: Clec11a deficiency did not affect the rate of BrdU incorporation by mesenchymal stem and progenitor cell populations identified based on CD51 and other markers.
source: Consistent with the data on LepR+ cells above, we did not detect any effect of Clec11a deficiency on the frequency of these cell populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G), their rate of BrdU incorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–M)
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–M.

claim: Clec11a deficiency did not affect the percentage of mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells that stained positively for activated caspase 3/7.
source: Consistent with the data on LepR+ cells above, we did not detect any effect of Clec11a deficiency on the frequency of these cell populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G), their rate of BrdU incorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–M), or the percentage of cells that stained positively for activated caspase 3/7 (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as data not shown.

claim: Clec11a is not required in vivo for the maintenance, survival, or the proliferation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Clec11a is therefore not required in vivo for the maintenance, survival, or the proliferation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple analyses showing no effects on progenitor frequency, proliferation, or survival.

claim: There was no difference in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies or in the number of cells per colony between Clec11a-/- and sex-matched littermate control mice at 2 and 10 months of age.
source: We observed no difference in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies or in the number of cells per colony (Figure 2—figure supplement 1T and U).
evidence: Supported by CFU-F colony formation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1T and U.

claim: Clec11a is not required for the maintenance of CFU-F in vivo or for their proliferation in culture.
source: Clec11a is therefore not required for the maintenance of CFU-F in vivo or for their proliferation in culture.
evidence: Conclusion based on normal CFU-F frequency and colony size in Clec11a-/- mice.

claim: Bone marrow stromal cells from Clec11a-/- mice gave rise to significantly fewer cells with alkaline phosphatase or alizarin red staining as compared to control cells under osteogenic culture conditions.
source: Consistent with the decreased osteogenesis in vivo, bone marrow stromal cells from Clec11a-/- mice gave rise to significantly fewer cells with alkaline phosphatase (a marker of mature osteoblasts and pre-adipocytes) or alizarin red (a marker of mineralization by mature osteoblasts) staining as compared to control cells under osteogenic culture conditions (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Clec11a deficiency did not significantly affect the expression of Sp7 (Osterix), Runx2, or Col1a1 in osteogenic cultures.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of cells in these cultures showed that Clec11a deficiency did not significantly affect the expression of Sp7 (Osterix), Runx2, or Col1a1 but did significantly reduce the expression of Integrin binding sialoprotein (Ibsp) and Dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Clec11a deficiency significantly reduced the expression of Integrin binding sialoprotein (Ibsp) and Dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1) in osteogenic cultures.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of cells in these cultures showed that Clec11a deficiency did not significantly affect the expression of Sp7 (Osterix), Runx2, or Col1a1 but did significantly reduce the expression of Integrin binding sialoprotein (Ibsp) and Dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Sp7, Runx2, and Col1a1 are broadly expressed by immature osteogenic progenitors and osteoblasts.
source: Sp7, Runx2, and Col1a1 are broadly expressed by immature osteogenic progenitors and osteoblasts (Jikko et al., 1999; Kulterer et al., 2007; Nakashima et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Jikko et al., 1999; Kulterer et al., 2007; Nakashima et al., 2002).

claim: Ibsp and Dmp1 mark mature osteoblasts.
source: Sp7, Runx2, and Col1a1 are broadly expressed by immature osteogenic progenitors and osteoblasts (Jikko et al., 1999; Kulterer et al., 2007; Nakashima et al., 2002) whereas Ibsp and Dmp1 mark mature osteoblasts (Kalajzic et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Kalajzic et al., 2005).

claim: Clec11a was required for the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
source: Clec11a was thus required for the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
evidence: Conclusion based on reduced mature osteoblast markers in Clec11a-/- cultures.

claim: Under adipogenic and chondrogenic culture conditions there was no difference between Clec11a-/- and control cells in terms of Oil Red O or Toluidine blue staining.
source: Under adipogenic (Figure 3E and F) and chondrogenic (Figure 3G and H) culture conditions we did not detect any difference between Clec11a-/- and control cells in terms of Oil Red O or Toluidine blue staining.
evidence: Supported by adipogenic and chondrogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 3E–H.

claim: The number of Perilipin+ adipocytes and Safranin O+ chondrocytes in femur sections from two month-old mice did not differ between Clec11a-/- and sex matched littermate control mice.
source: Consistent with this, the number of Perilipin+ adipocytes (Figure 3I–K) and Safranin O+ chondrocytes (Figure 3L–N) in femur sections from two month-old mice did not differ between Clec11a-/- and sex matched littermate control mice.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I–N.

claim: Significantly more adipocytes were observed in the femur sections from 10 month-old Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls.
source: However, we did observe significantly more adipocytes in the femur sections from 10 month-old Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The number of chondrocytes did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and littermate controls at 10 months of age.
source: The number of chondrocytes did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and littermate controls at 10 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Ossicles generated from Clec11a-/- cells contained significantly less bone as compared to the ossicles generated from control cells eight weeks after transplantation.
source: Eight weeks after transplantation, ossicles generated from Clec11a-/- cells contained significantly less bone as compared to the ossicles generated from control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: Supported by ossicle formation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1P.

claim: The number of adipocytes per unit area did not differ between ossicles containing Clec11a-/- as compared to control cells.
source: In contrast, the number of adipocytes per unit area did not differ between ossicles containing Clec11a-/- as compared to control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: Supported by ossicle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: Two weeks after fracture, Clec11a-/- mice had significantly less callus bone around the fracture site as compared to controls.
source: Two weeks later, Clec11a-/- mice had significantly less callus bone around the fracture site (Figure 4A) and significantly more callus cartilage (Figure 4B) as compared to controls, suggesting delayed endochondral ossification.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Two weeks after fracture, Clec11a-/- mice had significantly more callus cartilage as compared to controls.
source: Two weeks later, Clec11a-/- mice had significantly less callus bone around the fracture site (Figure 4A) and significantly more callus cartilage (Figure 4B) as compared to controls, suggesting delayed endochondral ossification.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduced callus bone and increased callus cartilage in Clec11a-/- mice two weeks after fracture suggests delayed endochondral ossification.
source: Two weeks later, Clec11a-/- mice had significantly less callus bone around the fracture site (Figure 4A) and significantly more callus cartilage (Figure 4B) as compared to controls, suggesting delayed endochondral ossification.
evidence: Inference based on histological observations of reduced bone and increased cartilage in callus.

claim: MicroCT analysis of the callus at the fracture site two weeks after the fracture revealed significantly reduced trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular thickness, and trabecular connectivity density in Clec11a-/- bones.
source: MicroCT analysis of the callus at the fracture site two weeks after the fracture revealed significantly reduced trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular thickness, and trabecular connectivity density (Figure 4C–H) and significantly increased trabecular spacing (Figure 4I) in Clec11a-/- bones.
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 4C–H.

claim: MicroCT analysis of the callus at the fracture site two weeks after the fracture revealed significantly increased trabecular spacing in Clec11a-/- bones.
source: MicroCT analysis of the callus at the fracture site two weeks after the fracture revealed significantly reduced trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular thickness, and trabecular connectivity density (Figure 4C–H) and significantly increased trabecular spacing (Figure 4I) in Clec11a-/- bones.
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The bone mineral density in the callus did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and control mice two weeks after fracture.
source: The bone mineral density in the callus did not significantly differ between Clec11a-/- and control mice (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The callus volume, diameter, and polar moment of inertia were significantly increased in Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls two weeks after fracture.
source: The callus volume, diameter, and polar moment of inertia were significantly increased in Clec11a-/- mice as compared to littermate controls (Figure 4K–M), further suggesting that fracture healing was compromised in Clec11a-/- mice (O'Neill et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 4K–M, with interpretation supported by citation to O'Neill et al., 2012.

claim: Addition of rClec11a to cultures of wild-type bone marrow stromal cells significantly increased alizarin red staining, suggesting increased mineralization.
source: Addition of rClec11a to these cultures significantly increased alizarin red staining, suggesting increased mineralization (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Addition of rClec11a rescued osteogenesis by Clec11a-/- bone marrow stromal cells at 7 and 14 days after induction of differentiation.
source: Addition of rClec11a also rescued osteogenesis by Clec11a-/- bone marrow stromal cells at 7 and 14 days after induction of differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–M.

claim: Transient expression of mouse Clec11a cDNA in the MC3T3-E1 mouse pre-osteoblast cell line increased osteogenic differentiation by these cells in culture.
source: Transient expression of mouse Clec11a cDNA in the MC3T3-E1 mouse pre-osteoblast cell line (Wang et al., 1999) increased osteogenic differentiation by these cells in culture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: Addition of rClec11a to cultures of sorted LepR+CD105+CD45-Ter119-CD31- cells did not significantly affect the percentage of cells that formed CFU-F or the number of cells per colony.
source: Addition of rClec11a to these cultures did not significantly affect the percentage of cells that formed CFU-F or the number of cells per colony (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by CFU-F colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Upon induction of differentiation, rClec11a significantly increased the number of alkaline phosphatase positive osteoblasts per colony.
source: Upon induction of differentiation, rClec11a significantly increased the number of alkaline phosphatase positive osteoblasts per colony (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: rClec11a did not significantly affect the frequencies of dividing osteoblasts or osteoblasts undergoing apoptosis within the colonies.
source: This appeared to reflect a promotion of differentiation as rClec11a did not significantly affect the frequencies of dividing osteoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) or osteoblasts undergoing apoptosis within the colonies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation and caspase-3/7 activity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Addition of rClec11a did not significantly affect Sp7, Runx2, or Col1a1 expression by cells within osteogenic cultures, but it did significantly increase the expression of Ibsp and Dmp1.
source: Consistent with the experiments above, addition of rClec11a did not significantly affect Sp7, Runx2, or Col1a1 expression by cells within these cultures, but it did significantly increase the expression of Ibsp and Dmp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Clec11a is sufficient to promote the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
source: Clec11a is thus sufficient to promote the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experiments showing rClec11a increases mature osteoblast markers without affecting proliferation or survival.

claim: rClec11a dose-dependently increased trabecular bone volume in the distal femur metaphysis of two month-old wild-type mice after 28 days of daily subcutaneous injections.
source: Consistent with the in vitro data, rClec11a dose-dependently increased trabecular bone volume in the distal femur metaphysis (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The higher doses of rClec11a significantly increased trabecular number and reduced trabecular spacing in two month-old wild-type mice after 28 days of daily subcutaneous injections.
source: The higher doses of rClec11a also significantly increased trabecular number and reduced trabecular spacing (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: The increased osteogenesis by rClec11a was associated with a significantly increased mineralized bone surface and bone formation rate, but did not affect bone resorption.
source: The increased osteogenesis was associated with a significantly increased mineralized bone surface (Figure 5H) and bone formation rate (Figure 5I), but did not affect bone resorption (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by calcein labeling and bone resorption marker data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: Cortical bone parameters in the femur diaphysis were not affected by rClec11a in wild-type mice after 28 days of daily subcutaneous injections.
source: Cortical bone parameters in the femur diaphysis were not affected by rClec11a in these experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N–S).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1N–S.

claim: rClec11a promotes osteogenesis in wild-type mice in vivo.
source: rClec11a thus promotes osteogenesis in wild-type mice in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased trabecular bone volume and bone formation rate after rClec11a administration.

claim: Daily subcutaneous injections of 50 µg/kg rClec11a to six month-old Clec11a-/- mice for 28 days restored plasma Clec11a to control levels.
source: To test whether administration of rClec11a can rescue the bone loss phenotype in Clec11a-/- mice, we administered daily subcutaneous injections of 50 µg/kg rClec11a to six month-old Clec11a-/- mice for 28 days. This restored plasma Clec11a to control levels (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as data not shown.

claim: Clec11a-/- mice exhibited significantly increased trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular thickness, connectivity density, and decreased trabecular spacing after 28 days of daily subcutaneous injections of 50 µg/kg rClec11a.
source: Consistent with this, Clec11a-/- mice exhibited significantly increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 5K and L), trabecular number, trabecular thickness, connectivity density, and decreased trabecular spacing (Figure 5M–Q).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 5K–Q.

claim: After rClec11a administration to Clec11a-/- mice, trabecular bone parameters were similar to those in normal control mice.
source: After rClec11a administration to Clec11a-/- mice, trabecular bone parameters were similar to those in normal control mice.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of trabecular bone parameters after rClec11a treatment.

claim: Ovariectomy in adult mice induces osteoporosis by increasing bone resorption.
source: Ovariectomy in adult mice induces osteoporosis by increasing bone resorption (Rodan and Martin, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Rodan and Martin, 2000).

claim: MicroCT analysis showed that trabecular bone volume and number were significantly reduced in ovariectomized mice while trabecular spacing was significantly increased.
source: MicroCT analysis showed that trabecular bone volume and number were significantly reduced in ovariectomized mice (Figure 6A–C) while trabecular spacing was significantly increased (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6A–E.

claim: Daily administration of PTH to ovariectomized mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume and trabecular number, while reducing trabecular spacing.
source: Daily administration of PTH to ovariectomized mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 6B) and trabecular number (Figure 6C), while reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6B, C, and E.

claim: Ovariectomy did not significantly affect the plasma Clec11a level.
source: Ovariectomy did not significantly affect the plasma Clec11a level (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as data not shown.

claim: Daily administration of rClec11a to ovariectomized mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume and trabecular number, while reducing trabecular spacing.
source: Daily administration of rClec11a to ovariectomized mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 6B) and trabecular number (Figure 6C), while reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6B, C, and E.

claim: Cortical bone parameters were not significantly changed by PTH or Clec11a administration in ovariectomized mice.
source: Cortical bone parameters were not significantly changed by PTH or Clec11a administration in these experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: rClec11a can prevent the loss of trabecular bone in ovariectomized mice.
source: rClec11a can therefore prevent the loss of trabecular bone in ovariectomized mice.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased trabecular bone parameters after rClec11a administration to ovariectomized mice.

claim: The urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline was significantly increased in ovariectomized mice as compared to sham operated controls.
source: Consistent with the fact that ovariectomy increases bone resorption (Harada and Rodan, 2003), the urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline was significantly increased in ovariectomized mice as compared to sham operated controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by bone resorption marker data shown in Figure 6F, with interpretation supported by citation to Harada and Rodan, 2003.

claim: Administration of rClec11a or PTH did not significantly affect deoxypyridinoline levels or numbers of osteoclasts in ovariectomized mice.
source: Administration of rClec11a or PTH did not significantly affect deoxypyridinoline levels (Figure 6F) or numbers of osteoclasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) in ovariectomized mice.
evidence: Supported by bone resorption marker and histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The trabecular bone formation rate and the number of osteoblasts associated with trabecular bones were significantly increased by rClec11a or PTH administration in ovariectomized mice.
source: However, based on calcein double labeling and histomorphometry analysis, the trabecular bone formation rate (Figure 6G) and the number of osteoblasts associated with trabecular bones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H) were significantly increased by rClec11a or PTH administration.
evidence: Supported by calcein labeling and histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: rClec11a prevented the loss of trabecular bone in ovariectomized mice by promoting bone formation.
source: rClec11a thus prevented the loss of trabecular bone in ovariectomized mice by promoting bone formation.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased bone formation rate and osteoblast numbers without affecting bone resorption.

claim: Daily intraperitoneal administration of 20 mg/kg dexamethasone for four weeks in mice significantly reduced lymphocyte numbers in the blood without significantly affecting neutrophil or monocyte counts.
source: Daily intraperitoneal administration of 20 mg/kg dexamethasone for four weeks in mice significantly reduced lymphocyte numbers in the blood without significantly affecting neutrophil or monocyte counts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by blood cell count data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: MicroCT analysis of the distal femur metaphysis showed significantly reduced trabecular bone volume and thickness in the dexamethasone-treated as compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: MicroCT analysis of the distal femur metaphysis showed significantly reduced trabecular bone volume and thickness in the dexamethasone-treated as compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 6H–L).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6H–L.

claim: Treatment of dexamethasone-treated mice with PTH significantly increased trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, and trabecular thickness while significantly reducing trabecular spacing.
source: Treatment of dexamethasone-treated mice with PTH significantly increased trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, and trabecular thickness while significantly reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 6H–L).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6H–L.

claim: Dexamethasone treatment did not significantly affect plasma Clec11a levels.
source: Dexamethasone treatment did not significantly affect plasma Clec11a levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2K)
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Administration of rClec11a to dexamethasone-treated mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume and trabecular number while significantly reducing trabecular spacing.
source: Dexamethasone treatment did not significantly affect plasma Clec11a levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2K), but administration of rClec11a to dexamethasone-treated mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume and trabecular number while significantly reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 6H–L).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6H–L.

claim: Dexamethasone treatment significantly reduced cortical thickness but neither PTH nor rClec11a rescued this effect.
source: Dexamethasone treatment also significantly reduced cortical thickness but neither PTH nor rClec11a rescued this effect in these experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–J).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–J.

claim: Dexamethasone reduces bone formation.
source: Consistent with the fact that dexamethasone reduces bone formation (Harada and Rodan, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Harada and Rodan, 2003).

claim: The rate of trabecular bone formation and the numbers of osteoblasts in trabecular bone were significantly reduced in dexamethasone-treated as compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Consistent with the fact that dexamethasone reduces bone formation (Harada and Rodan, 2003), the rate of trabecular bone formation based on calcein double labeling (Figure 6M) and the numbers of osteoblasts in trabecular bone (Figure 6—figure supplement 2L) were significantly reduced in dexamethasone-treated as compared to vehicle-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by calcein labeling and histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6M and Figure 6—figure supplement 2L.

claim: Administration of PTH or rClec11a significantly increased the trabecular bone formation rate and the number of osteoblasts in dexamethasone-treated mice.
source: Administration of PTH or rClec11a significantly increased the trabecular bone formation rate (Figure 6M) and the number of osteoblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2L) in dexamethasone-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by calcein labeling and histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6M and Figure 6—figure supplement 2L.

claim: Dexamethasone treatment, or administration of PTH or rClec11a, did not significantly affect deoxypyridinoline levels or osteoclast numbers.
source: As expected, dexamethasone treatment, or administration of PTH or rClec11a, did not significantly affect deoxypyridinoline levels (Figure 6N) or osteoclast numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: Supported by bone resorption marker and histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6N and Figure 6—figure supplement 2M.

claim: rClec11a prevented the loss of trabecular bone in dexamethasone-treated mice by promoting bone formation.
source: rClec11a thus prevented the loss of trabecular bone in dexamethasone-treated mice by promoting bone formation.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased bone formation rate and osteoblast numbers without affecting bone resorption.

claim: Daily administration of PTH to ovariectomized mice (starting 4 weeks after ovariectomy) increased trabecular bone volume and significantly reduced trabecular spacing relative to untreated ovariectomized mice.
source: Daily administration of PTH to ovariectomized mice increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 7B) and significantly reduced trabecular spacing relative to untreated ovariectomized mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 7B and E.

claim: PTH treatment significantly increased cortical area and cortical thickness in ovariectomized mice (starting 4 weeks after ovariectomy).
source: PTH treatment also significantly increased cortical area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and cortical thickness (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: Daily administration of rClec11a to ovariectomized mice (starting 4 weeks after ovariectomy) significantly increased trabecular bone volume and trabecular number, while reducing trabecular spacing relative to untreated ovariectomized mice.
source: Daily administration of rClec11a to ovariectomized mice significantly increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 7B) and trabecular number (Figure 7C), while reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 7E) relative to untreated ovariectomized mice.
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 7B, C, and E.

claim: rClec11a did not significantly affect cortical area or cortical thickness in ovariectomized mice (starting 4 weeks after ovariectomy).
source: rClec11a did not significantly affect cortical area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) or cortical thickness (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) in ovariectomized mice.
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: rClec11a can reverse trabecular bone loss after the onset of ovariectomy-induced osteoporosis.
source: rClec11a can thus reverse trabecular bone loss after the onset of ovariectomy-induced osteoporosis.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased trabecular bone parameters when rClec11a was administered 4 weeks after ovariectomy.

claim: Addition of rhClec11a to human bone marrow stromal cells cultured under osteogenic culture conditions significantly increased osteoblast differentiation based on alkaline phosphatase and alizarin red staining.
source: Addition of rhClec11a to human bone marrow stromal cells cultured under osteogenic culture conditions significantly increased osteoblast differentiation based on alkaline phosphatase (Figure 7H and I) and alizarin red staining (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data shown in Figure 7H–K.

claim: rhClec11a significantly accelerated bone formation in the ossicles after four weeks and significantly increased bone formation in the ossicles after eight weeks.
source: rhClec11a significantly accelerated bone formation in the ossicles after four weeks and significantly increased bone formation in the ossicles after eight weeks (Figure 7L–O).
evidence: Supported by ossicle formation assay data shown in Figure 7L–O.

claim: rhClec11a promotes osteogenesis by human bone marrow stromal cells in vivo.
source: rhClec11a thus promotes osteogenesis by human bone marrow stromal cells in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion based on increased bone formation in ossicles after rhClec11a administration.

claim: Clec11a is a new osteogenic factor which maintains the adult skeleton by promoting osteogenesis.
source: We have identified a new osteogenic factor, Clec11a, which maintains the adult skeleton by promoting the osteogenesis.
evidence: Summary statement based on all experimental findings in the study.

claim: Clec11a was necessary and sufficient to promote osteogenesis in culture and in vivo.
source: Clec11a was necessary and sufficient to promote osteogenesis in culture and in vivo.
evidence: Summary statement based on loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Clec11a deficiency significantly reduced bone volume in both limb bones and vertebrae of adult mice.
source: Clec11a deficiency significantly reduced bone volume in both limb bones and vertebrae of adult mice (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by microCT analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin appears to promote bone formation by promoting the differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
source: Clec11a/Osteolectin appears to promote bone formation by promoting the differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple differentiation experiments.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin deficient bone marrow stromal cells formed significantly fewer osteoblasts and mineralized bone matrix in culture with significantly lower expression of the mature osteoblast markers Ibsp and Dmp1.
source: Clec11a/Osteolectin deficient bone marrow stromal cells formed significantly fewer osteoblasts and mineralized bone matrix in culture (Figure 3A–D) with significantly lower expression of the mature osteoblast markers Ibsp and Dmp1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Addition of recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin to cultures of wild-type bone marrow stromal cells significantly increased the formation of osteoblasts as well as Ibsp and Dmp1 expression.
source: Addition of recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin to cultures of wild-type bone marrow stromal cells significantly increased the formation of osteoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) as well as Ibsp and Dmp1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and G.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin deficient bone marrow stromal cells formed less bone in the ossicles in vivo.
source: Clec11a/Osteolectin deficient bone marrow stromal cells also formed less bone in the ossicles in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1O–Q).
evidence: Supported by ossicle formation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1O–Q.

claim: Recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin promoted bone formation in the ossicles in vivo.
source: Recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin promoted bone formation in the ossicles in vivo (Figure 7L–O).
evidence: Supported by ossicle formation assay data shown in Figure 7L–O.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin deficiency did not affect the frequency, proliferation, or survival of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors in vivo.
source: In contrast to its effects on osteogenic differentiation, Clec11a/Osteolectin deficiency did not affect the frequency, proliferation, or survival of bone marrow mesenchymal progenitors in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–M).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and proliferation/survival assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–M.

claim: Recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin did not have any effect on the frequency of CFU-F that formed colonies in culture or the number of cells per colony.
source: Recombinant Clec11a/Osteolectin also did not have any effect on the frequency of CFU-F that formed colonies in culture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or the number of cells per colony (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by CFU-F colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors but not their proliferation or survival.
source: We conclude that Clec11a/Osteolectin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors but not their proliferation or survival.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experiments showing effects on differentiation but not proliferation or survival.

claim: Hypertrophic chondrocytes can transdifferentiate into osteoblasts and osteocytes during endochondral ossification.
source: Hypertrophic chondrocytes can also transdifferentiate into osteoblasts and osteocytes during endochondral ossification (Ono et al., 2014b; Yang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Ono et al., 2014b; Yang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014b).

claim: In addition to promoting the differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts, Clec11a/Osteolectin might also promote the transdifferentiation of hypertrophic chondrocytes into osteoblasts.
source: Thus, in addition to promoting the differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors into mature osteoblasts, Clec11a/Osteolectin might also promote the transdifferentiation of hypertrophic chondrocytes into osteoblasts.
evidence: Speculation based on Clec11a expression in hypertrophic chondrocytes and known transdifferentiation potential.

claim: Lineage tracing studies will be required in future to test whether Clec11a/Osteolectin promotes the transdifferentiation of hypertrophic chondrocytes into osteoblasts.
source: Lineage tracing studies will be required in future to test this.
evidence: Statement about future experimental needs.

claim: Nobody has yet identified the receptor for Clec11a/Osteolectin.
source: Nobody has yet identified the receptor for Clec11a/Osteolectin, limiting our ability to study the signaling mechanisms by which it promotes osteogenesis.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge.

claim: Flag-tagged Clec11a/Osteolectin binds to the surface of osteogenic cell lines.
source: We do observe binding of flag-tagged Clec11a/Osteolectin to the surface of osteogenic cell lines (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as data not shown.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors by binding to a signaling receptor on the surface of these cells.
source: We hypothesize that Clec11a/Osteolectin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors by binding to a signaling receptor on the surface of these cells.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed binding to cell surfaces.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin is most closely related to Clec3b/Tetranectin based on phylogenic analysis.
source: Phylogenic analysis showed that Clec11a/Osteolectin is most closely related to Clec3b/Tetranectin.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Tetranectin expression increases during mineralization by osteogenic progenitors in culture.
source: Tetranectin expression increases during mineralization by osteogenic progenitors in culture and overexpression of Tetranectin in PC12 cells increases the bone content of tumors formed by these cells (Wewer et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Wewer et al., 1994).

claim: Overexpression of Tetranectin in PC12 cells increases the bone content of tumors formed by these cells.
source: Tetranectin expression increases during mineralization by osteogenic progenitors in culture and overexpression of Tetranectin in PC12 cells increases the bone content of tumors formed by these cells (Wewer et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Wewer et al., 1994).

claim: Tetranectin deficient mice exhibit kyphosis as a result of asymmetric growth plate development in vertebrae.
source: Tetranectin deficient mice exhibit kyphosis as a result of asymmetric growth plate development in vertebrae (Iba et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study (Iba et al., 2001).

claim: It is unknown whether Tetranectin is required for osteogenesis in vivo.
source: Tetranectin deficient mice exhibit kyphosis as a result of asymmetric growth plate development in vertebrae (Iba et al., 2001); however, it is unknown whether Tetranectin is required for osteogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge.

claim: Tetranectin is found in both cartilaginous fish and bony fish but Clec11a/Osteolectin is only found in bony fish and higher vertebrate species.
source: Tetranectin is found in both cartilaginous fish and bony fish but Clec11a/Osteolectin is only found in bony fish and higher vertebrate species.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Clec11a/Osteolectin evolved in bony species to promote osteogenic differentiation and mineralization.
source: This suggests that Clec11a/Osteolectin evolved in bony species to promote osteogenic differentiation and mineralization.
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic distribution of Clec11a/Osteolectin.

claim: Human and mouse Clec11a/Osteolectin proteins are 85% identical and 90% similar.
source: Among mammals Clec11a/Osteolectin is highly conserved: human and mouse Clec11a/Osteolectin proteins are 85% identical and 90% similar.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Recombinant human Clec11a/Osteolectin promoted osteogenesis by human bone marrow stromal cells in culture and in vivo.
source: Consistent with this, recombinant human Clec11a/Osteolectin promoted osteogenesis by human bone marrow stromal cells in culture and in vivo (Figure 7H–O).
evidence: Supported by osteogenic differentiation and ossicle formation assay data shown in Figure 7H–O.
